text: Over one week, three different users log three separate Incidents, all describing the same symptom: an intermittent VPN disconnect, roughly every 45 to 60 minutes, remote staff only. Each gets triaged and worked individually at first — nobody looks like a major outage on their own. By the third report in four days, the pattern is obvious.

The agent working that third Incident checks for an existing Problem matching VPN disconnect, finds none, and that's the trigger. A new Problem record gets created — short description naming the symptom and the interval — state set to New.

Next, each of the three Incidents gets its problem_id field set to point at this new Problem. That's the step that actually realizes the value from Lesson 6: the Problem's related list now shows all three Incidents together, three users, three timestamps, one shared pattern, with nobody having to go ask around.

The Problem moves to Root Cause Analysis. cause_notes gets updated incrementally — first a note correlating the pattern with concentrator load at peak login, then a note ruling out individual devices, then a note narrowing the cause to a specific concentrator's session-timeout configuration. Each note stays in order, so anyone reviewing later sees the reasoning, not just the final answer.

The concentrator setting is the confirmed cause, but changing it requires a scheduled Change — it can't just be flipped in production. With the cause confirmed and no permanent fix deployed, the Problem is flagged Known Error, and a workaround gets documented separately from the investigative notes.

Two days later, a fourth user reports the same symptom. Because the Known Error is now documented and surfaced through search, the agent finds it fast, applies the workaround, links this Incident's problem_id to the same Problem, and resolves it quickly — no re-investigation. The Problem itself stays in Known Error, not Resolved, because the concentrator setting still hasn't actually changed.

Once the scheduled Change adjusts that setting and the fix is verified, fix_notes records the permanent fix and the Problem moves to Resolved, then Closed. All four linked Incidents stay exactly as they were, each resolved at its own time, but every one of them still shows, via problem_id, that they were symptoms of one cause that's now actually fixed. Next, we move into Chapter 3 and the Change that would have deployed that fix: standard, normal, and emergency Changes.
